accuracy.evidence: Content follows the PSHE Association Programme of Study (2020) KS1 relationships strand (recognise when they or others feel lonely and what to do), the DfE Relationships Education guidance (2019) on caring friendships (friendships have ups and downs; how to seek help when a friendship makes them unhappy) and the DfE Health Education guidance (isolation and loneliness affect children; it is very important to discuss feelings with an adult). The 'keeps happening or on purpose: tell a grown-up' line matches the Anti-Bullying Alliance definition of bullying as repetitive, intentional hurting that can include leaving someone out. The lesson never says a child must not tell a grown-up after a one-off: the sort feedback, kid text and m9 all say telling a grown-up how you feel is always allowed. Parameterised items checked at corners: n 1 to 4 (p2), 5-n gives 4 to 1 (p4), n+k gives 2 to 4 (m5).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips adults see at this age: 'I don't care' taken at face value (prediction 1, m1 and the 'hide' refusal), hurting back as a way in (prediction 2, the 'Knock their tower down' refusal with its consequence), mean words back ('You're not my friend!' refused), standing and staring until the group gives in (challenge), a friend playing with someone new read as the end of the friendship (challenge, m3), keeping deliberate, repeated exclusion secret (prediction 3 and the 'again' refusal), and not noticing other children on their own (map scene: busy groups refused with 'look for someone on their own').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagleftout is built on this topic's own sequence: a thought cloud that only takes feeling words that match Mia's posture, a Helps box with a heart that fills only for steps that help, a playground map where Mia is dragged to the two children who are alone (busy groups refuse with their own reason), a once versus keeps-happening sort with a grown-up figure on the second tray, and a three-line personal plan. It differs from 372 flagentry (watching a game and asking well), 1065 flagsecret and 1066 flagstrength; the 6-token shingle check against every flag lab is at most 3%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is met by doing: 'Proud' bounces off the cloud with 'Mia is on her own and her head is down', so the learner reads the body clues; 'Knock their tower down' is refused with what happens next (they get cross, she is in trouble too), so the cost of hurting back is discovered; dragging Mia to the full game is refused and she is sent to look around, which leads to Ben and Lily; dropping 'The game was full today' on the grown-up tray explains once versus a pattern while saying she can still tell a grown-up; the plan only accepts each chip on its own line.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'Mia says I don't care. Does that mean she feels fine?' (Yes is tempting; the scene shows her head down and the words that fit are left out, lonely, sad); 'If Mia knocks their tower down, will they want to play with her?' (Yes, then they will see her, is a common child belief; the refusal shows the consequence); 'Jo says Nobody play with Mia every day. Should Mia keep it to herself?' (Yes, it is only a game; the sort puts it under tell a grown-up).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Clicked through all seven challenge questions at 390 px: each wrong answer names its own slip, for example 'Stand and stare until they let him in' gets 'Staring until they give in is not asking. If the game is full, find someone else.', 'Yes, she is not his friend now' gets 'Friends can play with other people too. It does not mean the friendship is over.', 'Keep it a secret' gets 'When it happens every day, it is not a thing to keep secret', and 'Walk past him' gets 'Sam may feel left out too.' Answer order rotates per question.

readability.evidence: Kid text Flesch-Kincaid grade about 0 (limit 5.0 for family lessons), adult text 8.6 (limit 10.0). Short sentences and everyday words: left out, sad, lonely, ask, find, tell a grown-up. Canvas labels are two to six words; scene feedback is one or two short sentences.

no_filler.evidence: No filler phrases (gate clean). Every kid paragraph carries one step of the plan (name the feeling; pick a helpful step; do not hurt back or hide; look around and tell a grown-up if it keeps happening). Adult text gives the curriculum basis, why the lab is ordered as it is, the common mistakes and how this lesson differs from Asking to join in.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for all five scenes after Show me: six feeling cards in a 2 x 3 grid under Mia and her cloud, six step cards under the Helps box (filled box lists three short ticks), the playground map with four labelled groups and Mia at the bottom (tree moved so it no longer covers Lily), six story cards over two trays with readable wrapped text, and the three plan lines with ten chips in a 2 x 5 grid. Real mouse drags at 390 px worked for word to cloud, step to Helps, Mia to Ben and Lily, story to tray and chip to line.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: one button per feeling word ('Mia feels lonely'), per next step, 'Go to Ben' style buttons for the map, 'Once: Game full' and 'Keeps happening: Game full' pairs with full-sentence aria-labels for the sort, and one button per plan chip. The canvas aria-label carries the scene description and every piece of feedback; challenge feedback is a role=status live region; ticks, crosses, a filling heart and faces mark state as well as colour; the browser gate runs axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) in both themes.

sources: PSHE Association (2020) Programme of Study for PSHE Education, Key stages 1 to 5: KS1 relationships (recognise when they or someone else feels lonely and what to do)
DfE (2019) Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education and Health Education: statutory guidance (caring friendships; mental wellbeing: isolation and loneliness, talking to an adult)
Anti-Bullying Alliance: definition of bullying (repetitive, intentional hurting, including leaving someone out)
